summary: Explains where RSVP and the related integrated services protocols fit, and gives guidance for deploying resource reservation at the time. It is an informational statement rather than a protocol specification, discussing what the technology can and cannot do.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP is a signal a program sends to the routers on its path, asking them to set aside a guaranteed amount of bandwidth. This memo says where that works today and where it does not, and gives a cautious recommendation about where to try it first.

questions: what are the limitations of rsvp
subtitle: Where RSVP can usefully be deployed, and the three problems to settle first.

tldr.problem: RSVP lets an application ask for a guaranteed level of service, but the machinery it depends on was still being specified when it reached the standards track.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the four additional components RSVP needs, from the message formats for service parameters to the routers that classify and schedule packets, and then names the three open issues: scaling, security and policy control.
tldr.outcome: The recommendation is to start inside an intranet or with one provider and a small number of flows, and not on a high-bandwidth backbone, where the per-flow cost of RSVP does not scale.

facts.label: Policy objects in the RSVP specification

today: RFC 2208 is an Informational memo from September 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It accompanies the first submission of RSVP and the integrated services specifications onto the Internet standards track, and the memo says that it may be updated at the completion of the working group's charter.

sections.title: Introduction and the Components RSVP Needs
sections.content:
RSVP is a unicast and multicast signalling protocol, designed to install and maintain reservation state information at each router along the path of a stream of data. The state handled by RSVP is defined by services specified by the Integrated Services Working Group. Those services and RSVP are being introduced to the IETF standards track jointly, and from then on the acronym RSVP on its own is used as a shorthand for the signalling protocol combined with the integrated service specifications.

RSVP must be used in conjunction with several additional components. There are message formats in which parameters for desired services can be expressed, specified in a proposed standard set. There are router and host mechanisms, such as packet classification and scheduling and admission control algorithms, to implement one or both of the service models. There are message formats in which parameters for desired policies for admission control and resource use can be expressed, and the Policy objects in the RSVP protocol specification are optional at this time. And there are diversely located mechanisms implementing desired admission control policy functions, including authorization and other security mechanisms.

In the presence of some form of each of these components, RSVP-enabled applications can achieve differentiated qualities of service across IP networks. Networked multimedia applications, many of which require or will benefit from a predictable end-user experience, are likely to be the initial users of RSVP-signalled services. Because RSVP and the integrated services mark a significant change to the service model of IP networks, RSVP has received considerable interest and press in advance of its release as a standards track RFC, and at the time of writing many vendors of operating systems and routers are incorporating RSVP and integrated services into their products for near-future availability. The goal of the applicability statement is to describe those uses of the current specification that are known to be feasible, and to identify areas of limitation and ongoing chartered work addressing some of these limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP on its own only says what is wanted. The routers still have to be built to act on the request, and someone has to decide who is allowed to make it.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content:
The resource requirements, in processing and storage, for running RSVP on a router increase proportionally with the number of separate sessions, that is, RSVP reservations. Supporting numerous small reservations on a high-bandwidth link may therefore easily overtax the routers, and is inadvisable. Implementing the packet classification and scheduling capabilities currently used to provide differentiated services for reserved flows may also be very difficult for some router products, or on some of their high-speed interfaces such as OC-3 and above.

These scaling issues imply that it will generally not be appropriate to deploy RSVP on high-bandwidth backbones at the present time. Looking forward, the operators of such backbones will probably not choose to implement RSVP naively for each separate stream. Rather, techniques are being developed that will, at the edge of the backbone, aggregate together the streams that require special treatment, and within the backbone various less costly approaches would then be used to set aside resources for the aggregate as a whole, as a way of meeting the end-to-end requirements of individual flows. In the near term, various vendors are likely to use diverse approaches to the aggregation of reservations, and there is not currently chartered work in the IETF for the development of standards in this space. A BOF on Future Directions of Differential Services, on April 7, 1997 at the Memphis IETF, was to consider the IETF's next steps on this among other issues, and public documentation of aggregation techniques and experience is encouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: Every reservation costs the router memory and processing, so a backbone carrying thousands of streams would drown in them. The likely answer is to treat a group of streams as one reservation at the edge of the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RSVP working group's submission for Proposed Standard includes two security-related documents. One addresses denial of service and hijacking or theft of service attacks. The other addresses RSVP mechanisms for data flows that themselves use IP security.

The first document is proposed to protect against spoofed reservation requests arriving at RSVP routers, which might be used to obtain service for unauthorized parties or to lock up network resources in a denial of service attack. Modified and spoofed reservation requests are detected by the use of hop-by-hop MD5 checksums, in an Integrity Object, between RSVP neighbour routers. RSVP hop-by-hop authentication assumes that key management and distribution for routers is resolved and deployed, and until an effective key infrastructure is in place, manually keyed session integrity might be used.

That RSVP needs an effective key infrastructure among routers is not unique to RSVP: it is widely acknowledged that there are numerous denial of service attacks on the routing infrastructure, quite independent of RSVP, that will only be resolved by deployment of a key infrastructure. Theft of service risks will require the user to deploy with caution, and an elementary precaution is to configure management logging of new and changed filter specifications in RSVP-enabled infrastructure, for example the newFlow trap. The second security-related document provides a mechanism for carrying flows in which the transport and user octets have been encrypted. Although such encryption is highly beneficial to certain applications, it is not relevant to the functional security of RSVP or reservations.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a reservation request is just a message, someone could forge one and take bandwidth that is not theirs. The protection is a checksum between neighbouring routers, which in turn needs a way to manage keys.

sections.title: Policy Control
sections.content:
Policy control addresses the issue of who can, and who cannot, make reservations, once a reservation protocol can be used to set up unequal services. The RSVP specification defines a mechanism for transporting policy information along with reservations, but it does not define the policies themselves, and vendors have stated that they will use the RSVP-defined mechanism to implement proprietary policies.

The RSVP working group is chartered to specify a simple standardized policy object and complete simple mechanisms for session use of the Integrity object in the near future, and this applicability statement may be updated at the completion of that charter. Before any decision to deploy RSVP, it would be wise to ensure that the policy control available from a vendor is adequate for the intended usage. In addition to the lack of documented policy mechanisms in any of the policy areas, such as access control, authorization and accounting, the community has little experience with describing, setting and controlling policies that limit Internet service. It is therefore likely that vendor solutions will be revised often, particularly before the IETF has developed any policy specification.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP can carry a rule about who may reserve what, but the rule itself is left to the operator, and each vendor was expected to invent its own. That is the part most likely to change.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Given the current form of the RSVP specifications, multimedia applications to be run within an intranet are likely to be the first to benefit from RSVP, and SNA/DLSW is another application considered likely to benefit. Within the single or small number of related administrative domains of an intranet, scalability, security and access policy will be more manageable than in the global Internet, and risk will be more controllable. Use of RSVP and supporting components for small numbers of flows within a single Internet service provider is similar to an intranet use.

Current experience with RSVP has been collected only from test runs in limited testbeds and intranet deployment, so the memo recommends that people begin to use RSVP in production intranet or limited ISP environments, where benefits can be realized without having to resolve some of the issues described earlier. It quotes RFC 2026 on the use of Proposed Standard technology: implementors should treat Proposed Standards as immature specifications, and it is desirable to implement them in order to gain experience and to validate, test and clarify the specification, but since the content of Proposed Standards may be changed if problems are found or better solutions are identified, deploying implementations of such standards into a disruption-sensitive environment is not recommended.

General issues of scalability, security and policy control are the subjects of active research and development, as are a number of topics beyond this applicability statement, such as third-party setup of either reservations or differentiated service.
sections.plainLanguage: Start small, on a network you control, with a handful of flows. Try it to learn, not to run a service that matters.
